text: James Baxter Hunt Jr. (May 16, 1937 – December 18, 2025) was an American politician and attorney who served as the 69th and 71st governor of North Carolina from 1977 to 1985 and again from 1993 to 2001, making him the longest-serving governor in the state's history. He tied with former Ohio governor Jim Rhodes for the sixth-longest gubernatorial tenure in post-Constitutional U.S. history, totaling 5,838 days. His daughter, Rachel Hunt, is currently the Lieutenant Governor of North Carolina. Hunt was born in Greensboro, North Carolina, on May 16, 1937, to James Baxter Hunt, a soil conservationist, and Elsie Brame Hunt, a schoolteacher; the family later moved to a farm outside Wilson, North Carolina. He was raised in the Free Will Baptist Church and later converted to Presbyterianism. Hunt earned a B.S. in agricultural education and a M.S. in agricultural economics from North Carolina State College (now North Carolina State University), where he served as the second student to hold two terms as Student Body President. His master's thesis focused on the economic analysis of different tobacco production techniques. He received a J.D. from the University of North Carolina School of Law in 1964 and served as president of the Young Democratic Clubs of North Carolina (now Young Democrats of North Carolina). From 1964 to 1966, he worked as a Ford Foundation economic advisor in Nepal. After participating in state and national Democratic campaigns and conventions, Hunt ran successfully for lieutenant governor in 1972 and was sworn in on January 5, 1973. With the election of Republican James Holshouser as governor in 1972, the Democratic majority in the General Assembly elevated the lieutenant governor's office, increasing its salary from $5,000 to $30,000 per year, expanding its operating budget, and growing its staff from two to five. Hunt was first sworn in as governor on January 8, 1977, becoming the only North Carolina governor elected to four terms; he first won in 1976 over Republican David Flaherty and was re-elected in 1980, defeating I. Beverly Lake. During his first term, he supported a constitutional change allowing him to run for a second consecutive term. In 1981, he chaired the Hunt Commission, which established superdelegates in the Democratic National Convention. In 1984, he lost the U.S. Senate race to Jesse Helms and stepped away from elective politics for eight years before returning in 1992, defeating Republican lieutenant governor and Hardee's executive Jim Gardner. He was re-elected in 1996 by a large margin over future U.S. Congressman Robin Hayes and left office in January 2001, succeeded by Attorney General Mike Easley. In the 1970s, Hunt supported the Equal Rights Amendment and, with his wife Carolyn, urged its ratification by the state legislature (which failed by two votes), appointing Betty Ray McCain as chief lobbyist. He was an early advocate for teaching standards and early childhood education, gaining national recognition for the Smart Start program for pre-kindergarteners. In his book, First in America: An Education Governor Challenges North Carolina, Hunt stated that under his testing and accountability measures, test scores improved, with 56% of students proficient in 1994 compared to 70% in 2000, and warned that without testing students face a "limited future." In 2000, he was considered a possible Democratic nominee for Vice President or Education Secretary under Al Gore, and in 2004, Sen. John Kerry considered him for Secretary of Education if he won the presidential race; he was also considered a candidate for Barack Obama’s Secretary of Education. Hunt chaired the Carnegie Task Force on Teaching as a Profession, which created the National Board for Professional Teaching Standards, and served on the Spellings Commission on the Future of Higher Education. As governor, he promoted technology and economic development through the establishment of the North Carolina Biotechnology Center, the Centennial Campus of North Carolina State University, and the North Carolina School of Science and Mathematics. He played a key role in the trial of the Wilmington Ten; after CBS's 60 Minutes broadcast raised concerns about fabricated evidence, Hunt reduced their sentences from 20–25 years to 13–17 years in January 1978, rather than pardoning them. While many Black North Carolinian politicians disapproved, the general sentiment was that "right now blacks have nowhere else to turn," and Howard Nathaniel Lee refused to resign as Secretary of the North Carolina Department of Natural Resources and Community Development as protest. Hunt appointed both the first African American to the North Carolina Supreme Court, Henry Frye, and the first Black Cabinet member, Howard Lee. He supported the death penalty and rarely granted clemency, overseeing 13 executions during his terms—two in his first period and 11 in his second—including the first execution in North Carolina after the U.S. Supreme Court reinstated capital punishment in 1976 (James W. Hutchins) and the first nationwide execution of a woman in 22 years (Velma Barfield). Hunt was a strong proponent of North Carolina’s tobacco industry, even as health concerns grew; when U.S. Surgeon General Dr. C. Everett Koop accused the industry of targeting children and endangering lives, Hunt called for Koop’s impeachment. He founded and served as chair emeritus of the Institute for Emerging Issues at N.C. State University and in 2001 established the James B. Hunt Jr. Institute for Educational Leadership & Policy Foundation, Inc., commonly known as The Hunt Institute, dedicated to empowering governors, policymakers, and educational leaders in developing public education strategies. Hunt married Carolyn Leonard in 1958; they had a son, James Baxter Hunt III, and three daughters, including Rachel Hunt, who served as a former North Carolina state senator and, as of 2025, is the state’s Lieutenant Governor. Hunt died at his home in Lucama, North Carolina, on December 18, 2025, at the age of 88. Flags across North Carolina flew at half-staff from December 19, 2025, until his internment. Starting December 20, 2025, a condolence book at the North Carolina State Capitol was open for public signing and remained available through January 2, 2026. His funeral was held on December 26, 2025, at First Presbyterian Church in Wilson, North Carolina, with family, friends, and political figures from across the state in attendance; a reception and visitation followed, open to the public. Hunt was buried, and the condolence book remained accessible through January 2, 2026. Hunt ran unopposed in the Democratic primary. An authorized biography of Hunt, authored by advisor Gary Pearce, was released in 2010.
